Colonial and Puritan Literature: Puritanism
Belief system emphasising hard work, predestination, and human sinfulness
Plain style
Puritan writing valuing clarity and directness over ornament
Sermon
A religious speech intended to persuade and instruct a congregation
Jeremiad
A sermon lamenting moral decline and warning of judgement
Captivity narrative
An account of being taken prisoner, popular in colonial America
Providence
The Puritan belief that God directs all events
Typology
Reading events as fulfilments of biblical patterns
Anne Bradstreet
First published American poet, writing on family and faith
Jonathan Edwards
Preacher of Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God
Allusion
A reference to another text, person, or event
Revolutionary and Early National Writing: Rhetoric
The art of persuasive speaking and writing
Ethos
A persuasive appeal based on the speaker's credibility
Pathos
A persuasive appeal to the audience's emotions
Logos
A persuasive appeal based on logic and evidence
Aphorism
A short statement expressing a general truth
Declaration of Independence
Jefferson's argument for separation grounded in natural rights
Benjamin Franklin
Author of an influential autobiography built on self-improvement
Patrick Henry
Orator known for Give me liberty or give me death
Parallelism
Repeating grammatical structure for rhythm and emphasis
Rhetorical question
A question asked for effect rather than an answer
Romanticism and Transcendentalism: Movement valuing emotion, nature, imagination, and the individual
Belief in innate goodness, self-reliance, and truth found beyond the senses
Author of Walden and Civil Disobedience
Peaceful refusal to obey unjust laws
Emerson's idea of a universal spirit connecting all beings
Emphasis on personal independence over conformity
Romantic belief that the natural world reveals moral truth
Poetry without regular meter or rhyme
Poet of Leaves of Grass who pioneered free verse in America
Gothic and Dark Romanticism: Dark Romanticism
A strand of Romanticism exploring guilt, sin, and human darkness
Gothic literature
Writing using gloom, decay, and terror to create atmosphere
Edgar Allan Poe
Master of the Gothic tale and originator of detective fiction
Nathaniel Hawthorne
Novelist exploring Puritan guilt in The Scarlet Letter
Unreliable narrator
A narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted
Symbolism
Using an object to represent a larger abstract idea
Foreshadowing
Hints planted early about what will happen later
Mood
The emotional atmosphere a text creates in the reader
Single effect
Poe's principle that every element should serve one unified impression
Psychological realism
Focusing on the inner workings of a character's mind
Realism and Naturalism: Realism
Depicting ordinary life accurately, without romantic idealisation
Naturalism
An intense realism showing characters shaped by environment and heredity
Regionalism
Writing that captures the speech and customs of a specific place
Local color
Detail conveying the distinctive character of a region
Vernacular
Everyday spoken language used in writing
Mark Twain
Author of Huckleberry Finn, a landmark in American vernacular
Determinism
The naturalist view that forces beyond a character's control decide fate
Satire
Using humour and irony to criticise human failings
Verisimilitude
The quality of seeming true to life
Social criticism
Writing that exposes flaws in society
The Harlem Renaissance: Harlem Renaissance
1920s flowering of African American literature, music, and art
Langston Hughes
Poet who brought jazz and blues rhythms into verse
Zora Neale Hurston
Novelist and folklorist who recorded Black Southern speech
Double consciousness
Du Bois's idea of seeing oneself through the eyes of a hostile society
Blues poetry
Verse built on the repetition and structure of blues music
Jazz influence
Improvisation and syncopation shaping literary rhythm
The New Negro
Term for a generation asserting pride and cultural authority
Great Migration
Movement of Black Americans from the rural South to Northern cities
Dialect
Regional or social speech reproduced in writing
Refrain
A repeated line or phrase in a poem or song
Modernism: Modernism
Early twentieth-century movement breaking with traditional forms
Lost Generation
Writers disillusioned by the First World War
Stream of consciousness
Narration following the unfiltered flow of a character's thoughts
Fragmentation
Deliberately broken structure reflecting a disordered world
Imagism
Poetry built on precise, concrete images and spare language
F. Scott Fitzgerald
Chronicler of the Jazz Age in The Great Gatsby
Ernest Hemingway
Novelist known for stripped-down prose and understatement
Iceberg theory
Hemingway's idea that most meaning stays beneath the surface
Disillusionment
Loss of faith in inherited ideals, central to modernist writing
The American Dream
The belief that effort brings success, frequently interrogated in this era
Contemporary American Voices: Postmodernism
Writing that questions objective truth and plays with form
Metafiction
Fiction that draws attention to its own status as fiction
Magical realism
Realistic narrative containing accepted supernatural elements
Multicultural literature
Writing centring the experience of varied cultural communities
Memoir
A nonfiction account of a portion of the author's own life
Confessional poetry
Verse drawing directly on private personal experience
Voice in writing
The distinctive personality and style of an author
Intertextuality
The way texts refer to and depend on other texts
Unreliable memory
A narrator's recollection presented as incomplete or distorted
Identity in literature
Exploration of how culture, race, and gender shape the self
Rhetorical Analysis: Rhetorical analysis
Examining how a text persuades rather than just what it says
Speaker
The voice presenting the argument, real or constructed
Audience
The intended readers or listeners a text is shaped for
Purpose
What the writer wants the audience to think, feel, or do
Context
The circumstances surrounding a text that shape its meaning
Tone
The writer's attitude toward the subject
Diction
Word choice and its effect on meaning and tone
Syntax
Sentence structure and its rhetorical effect
Juxtaposition
Placing two ideas side by side to sharpen a contrast
Concession and rebuttal
Acknowledging an opposing point, then answering it
Anaphora
Repeating a word or phrase at the start of successive clauses
Research and Synthesis Writing: Synthesis
Combining several sources into one coherent argument
Thesis statement
The central claim a paper sets out to prove
Primary source
An original record from the time being studied
Secondary source
A later analysis or interpretation of primary material
Credible source
A source that is current, authoritative, and free of obvious bias
Plagiarism
Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own
Paraphrase
Restating a source fully in your own words, still cited
Direct quotation
Using a source's exact words inside quotation marks
MLA citation
The documentation style commonly used in English courses
Works Cited page
The alphabetical list of every source referenced
Counterargument
The strongest opposing view, addressed directly in your paper
Annotated bibliography
A source list with a short summary and evaluation of each entry
